see.b: This temple of the Tendai sect, constructed in 733, is nearly the oldest in the Tokyo area, second only to Sensoji in Asakusa. Although the temple building itself is modest, the surrounding village of food stands, soba restaurants and…

see.pr: Adults ¥500, seniors ¥250, junior high schoolers ¥200, children free
see.b: Something is always blooming in this large, all-season botanical garden. The park is divided into areas which feature specific plants such as plum and cherry blossom trees; the Japanese azalea garden and English-style rose garden are…
On the 25th on the month satokagura dance and music numbers are performed. The satokagura is a traditional Shinto dance.
This 50,000-seat soccer stadium is home field for Tokyo Verdy and FC Tokyo; American football, rugby games and flea markets can also be found here.
Large cinema complex with eleven screens and ~1,600 seats in total. Opened in 2017.
One of the oldest shrines in Tokyo. Kurayami Matsuri (night festival) is famous. Six large drums. Eight omikoshi (small shrines).

Japan's largest horse racing facility. Home to several prestigious Grade 1 events including the Yasuda Kinen and Japan Cup races. Racing on weekends only, generally late January-February, May-June and October-November, though you may…
A hot spa.
A popular spot to see summer fireworks.
The burial site of the Shōwa Emperor Hirohito and his predecessor, the Taishō Emperor Yoshihito.
Museum dedicated to optical illusion exhibits.
Ruins of a castle destroyed during the Warring States Period by Toyotama Hideyoshi. You can see Sagami Bay from the lookout at the mountaintop.
Grave of Matsugi Shichiro (松木七郎), a samurai during the Kamakura era. Small pagoda-like grave by a small shrine.
There are many festivals, especially the large summer festival.

A 600-meter peak that is easily accessible by a combination of cable car and hiking, giving a little taste of nature in Tokyo. It is popular in the autumn to see the changing color of the leaves, however springtime is also nice because…

The largest park near this station. On weekends lots of families come to picnic and play ball. Many people also bring their dogs. In spring, there's a lot of cherry blossoms. It is very beautiful, so this park is famous as a good park…

This park is so big and has lots of greenery. You can enjoy walking around while listening to birdsong. On weekends many people visit here. Moreover, there are Japanese rice fields (tanbo) and a water mill. There is a big pond named…
There are about 770 Maidenhair trees (ichou), and in autumn, they change color and it is very beautiful.
A fireworks festival.
An internet cafe. You can use computers, read books and you can play darts and billiards. A drink bar is included.
Information is only available in Japanese.
A live show venue. Shows are only in Japanese.

A large animation festival that occurs in mid-October every year. English-language tours of the festival may be available from tour operator H.I.S. The last edition to date was held in 2020, with its future unsure.
A park with sculptures scattered in the lush greenery and water.
Find Pokemon Manhole in the park in the city where Pokémon creator Satoshi Tajiri spent his childhood. The poke lid is a Pokémon Go pokestop.

see.n: Machida Yakushiike Park Shikisai no Mori.
see.b: Machida Yakushiike Park is made up of several areas.

see.h: Information and Direct sales office 09:00-17:00; cafe and restaurant 10:00-20:00; library lounge (rest area) 09:00-17:00; lab and experience workshop 09:00-19:3
see.b: There is a local food market, a cafe and restaurant where you can enjoy cooking with Machida's local ingredients, a workshop where you can try your hand at making crafts, and a park where you can enjoy a BBQ and a picnic empty-handed.

There is a pond called Yakushiike, where you can enjoy cherry blossoms and wisteria in the spring, irises and lotus in the summer, and autumn leaves in the fall. There is another small temple called Notuda Yakushido.There are also…

The Botanic Garden is a 7-minute walk north of Yakushi Pond. The park is open for a fee according to the blooming period of peonies and peonies (usually mid-April to early May). Free of charge except when the flowers are in bloom.

The Botanic Garden is a 10-minute walk north of Yakushi Pond. The garden is pay-per-open for a limited period of time from late April to early May when the orchid Calanthe discolor are in bloom. The park is opened free of charge during…

see.pr: ¥500; admission to the park is free for junior high school students and younger
see.b: The garden is pay-per-open for a limited period of time from early July to early November every year when the Dahlia are in bloom. The rest stop and flower shop are open all year round. (Closed Jan 1-3.)

Various farming equipment and agricultural tools on display. People of older generations are hopeful that their younger successors will carry on their farming traditions, hence this museum was built. The museum has a nice atmosphere.

see.h: Wed-Mon: Mar 16-Oct 15 10:00-17:00; Oct 16-Mar 15 10:00-16:00; Dec 1-26 10:00-15:00; closed Dec 27-Jan 2; closed first Tue-Fri in Jun, Sep, and Dec
see.b: A park with about 100 squirrels. Guests can get close to the squirrels, play with them, and give them food. Squirrel feed can be purchased for ¥100.

This is the world's only official satellite of the Schulz Museum of Art, the Peanuts fan's mecca in Santa Rosa, California, USA. Original drawings from "Peanuts" and a giant Snoopy sculpture are on display. There are workshops and a…

see.n: Machida City Museum of Graphic Arts
see.b: The only museum in Japan that focuses on prints. Weekdays 10:00-17:00 (admission is until 16:30) Saturdays, Sundays, and holidays 10:00-17:30 (admission is until 17:00) Closed every Monday and 28 Dec-4 Jan. Fees vary depending on the…
The former Shirasu residence. You can enjoy an old Japanese house and a beautiful garden. Inside the house is a museum.
The head of the family, Shikanosuke Kojima, was a close friend of Isami Kondo of the Shinsengumi, so there is a display of materials related to the Shinsengumi.
Japanese sword and armor of samurai from the Sengoku period are on display. There is also a life-size replica of a part of the famous Oda Nobunaga's castle.
It's a big library, so if you are looking for some books, you might find it here as it has a wide selection.

This is an Okinawan folk dance festival held annually. Many Eisa teams come to Machida. There are 23 pairs. The festival is very lively and fun, and various food items can be purchased from small stalls around the area.
A dining establishment with darts, card games, and board games. A nice place to have a party with friends.
A cafe with a twist — there are cats running around that you can play with. Great if you want to play with cats but not raise one long-term.
This place has a wide assortment of games, including bowling, karaoke, billiards, and many arcade games.
People worship the god of learning, Sugawara, at this shrine. In Heian period, Sahara was a scholar.
Holds 6,200 people. Many soccer games and university contests are held here.

see.a: 原町田2-7-3 トップヒルB1F
see.pr: Price depends on the event (normally includes 1 drink)
see.b: Live rock music, DJ live sets and dance performances throughout the week.

see.a: 中町１丁目１８−１５ クローヴビル1F
see.b: Live house in Machida. Schedule can be accessed on their website. It is also a music school during weekdays.
Live music and club, depending on the day.
This is the first genuine bicarbonate natural hot spring in Machida City, pumped up from 1,381 meters below ground.
A hot spring facility where you can take a day trip and stay overnight.

see.n: Tamasakai Natural Hot Springs Mori no Irodori
see.b: Surrounded by the rich natural environment of the Tama Hills and surrounded by greenery, you can enjoy an open-air bath with a flowing hot spring that has the effect of making your skin beautiful.
A J-League football club team based in Machida City. Machida Gion Stadium (Machida City Athletic Stadium) is their home ground.
An F-League futsal club team based in Machida City. Machida Sougo Taiikukan (Machida City General Gymnasium) is their home ground.
A Top-League rugby club team based in Machida City. Canon Sports Park is their home ground.

General Nogi's house is a great example of Western architecture constructed during the Meiji period (19th century), mixing Japanese and Western elements. The general killed himself here after the Meiji Emperor's death. Descend the…

Opened in April 2007, this competitor to Roppongi Hills boasts Tokyo's second tallest office building, a Ritz-Carlton and yet more endless acres of shopping and eating. Still, Midtown favors wood paneling and greenery over raw concrete…
Changing exhibitions devoted to the latest and greatest in Japanese design.
Fujifilm's exhibition space for the latest and greatest in photography. Exhibits are usually free and well worth a visit.
Hosts changing art exhibitions.

AKB48 is a home-grown, all-girl idol group — their name comes from Akihabara — which started in 2005 and quickly became the best-selling female group in Japan. They perform 6 days a week. If you are into J-pop music and cute girls all…

Akihabara's own temple. You can buy a multi-piece charm for ¥1,000 which will protect your electronic devices from evil. It's mostly noteworthy for the festival it organizes around May. On this occasion, a massive shrine is…
Another arcade, "Hey" on Chuo Dori is also run by Taito.
Formerly run by Sega, four locations in Akihabara. As of July 31, 2025, the first store of gigo was closed.

Up first, it features a much-photographed giant lantern and statues of guardian gods Raijin (god of thunder) and Fūjin (god of wind). First built in 942, the gate has been destroyed numerous times and the current incarnation dates to…
At the end of the arcade, it is the main gate, notable for a giant straw sandal (waraji) hung up on one side. This gate too is guarded by ferocious guardian gods. Rebuilt 1964.

Behind the gate, the main hall of the temple is perennially busy with a steady stream of worshippers wafting incense over themselves and trooping up the steps to pray and donate. According to legend, the hall was first built in 628 to…
It reputedly contains some of the ashes of the Buddha. Rebuilt 1973.

To the east behind the temple is this Shinto shrine devoted to protecting the Buddhist temple in a typically Japanese arrangement. The fairly plain shrine is not much to look at, but is notable as the focal point of the Sanja Matsuri…

If you turn left before the Hōzōmon gate and head west for a few hundred meters, this quiet shrine is on your left. The shrine is dedicated to the Japanese raccoon god tanuki, notably primarily for its big flask of sake and gigantic…

This temple next to Sensō-ji, to which it belongs, has a spectacular Japanese garden. While generally closed to the public, it opens for exhibitions most years from roughly mid-March to early May. Other than the small garden, which is…

Organized at Asakusa Jinja yearly on the third weekend in May, this is Tokyo's largest festival (matsuri) and attracts up to 2 million spectators. The main event is a procession known as Daigyōretsu, when traditional performers and…

Held on the last Saturday of August. The street parade, which features thousands of participants from all over Japan, is held in the afternoon around Sensō-ji, and there are some stage shows in the evening. The event started in 1981,…

The oldest amusement park in Japan. Next to the Sensō-ji temple grounds is this small and somewhat lackluster carnival complex with rides, booths, and games. The neighborhood theatre specializes in showing classic Japanese films, as…

Laid out in the 17th century, this splendid traditional garden boasts a large collection of trees and flowering plants that provide touches of beauty all year round. Winding paths, wooded hills, ponds teeming with ducks and fish. The…

A classical Japanese park with ponds, hills and teahouses, that was built in 1695 by Yanagisawa Yoshiyasu, a Tokugawa daimyo. It's a popular cherry blossom spot in spring and is lit up at night at this time.

eat.b: This lively izakaya restaurant specializes in pork, served on skewers like yakitori. The friendly staff will help you sample almost any part of the pig, including heart, liver, head meat and oesophagus, pointing to their own body to…

This is a cut-above curry restaurant which has several curries which put the usual Japanese fare to shame. Try ordering the set menu with dessert, rum-topped ice cream is a nice finish after spicy curry. The owner may try to speak some…

A Japanese woman runs the place by herself and serves traditional Japanese fare. Sets change by day and include a main dish and two sides, fruit, rice, miso soup, and coffee. Eat in and take out available.
A noodle shop. The base of this noodle is tonkotsu (pork bone). The noodles are thin. This shop has many kinds of interesting and unusual toppings: cheese, umeboshi, soft-boiled egg, and more.
A ramen shop.
An Italian restaurant.

The food doesn't challenge the non-Japanese palate too much — mostly chicken and sashimi, and to order you just pick one of three dinner sets. The great thing about this restaurant is the ambience. The restaurant comprises a…
For once, a pub in Tokyo that's English, not Irish.
Food and music from the Caribbean, South America, Africa, and Asia.

The abura soba served at this ramen restaurant is a welcome break from the usual salty and soupy ramen. Actually ramen not soba, abura soba is served with no soup, but does include the usual green onion, slice of pork, etc. An…

Famous for its ball-shaped deep-fried mincemeat cutlets (menchi katsu, ¥300 apiece) which you can get as take-out, and there's usually a long line of customers spilling out into the shopping arcade. Has a steakhouse upstairs.

In the Harmonica Alley, across from the Kichijoji Station, there is a little shop serving the uniquely Okinawan dish called taco rice. Taco meat and all the usual taco toppings, all over rice. Surprising and tasty!
This restaurant has an eclectic selection of Asian food and international interior decorations. The bizarre mixture of furniture from various countries and of assorted ages makes the mind boggle.
An Italian-style chain restaurant.

eat.a: 御殿山1-2-1 御殿山デュープレックスR'S 2階
eat.b: This restaurant serves western-style vegetarian and vegan sandwiches and salads. Oddly, the atmosphere is more reminiscent of a coffee shop near a college than a restaurant. Lights dangle from long cords from the ceiling and hover just…

This yakitori (grilled chicken) tavern is a Kichijoji institution, first opening in 1928. The interior scene could be straight out of a 1950s black-and-white movie, full of raucous salarymen drowning their troubles in tall glasses of…
This restaurant is small — only room for 20. However, the meat and fish are quite good, and the young and energetic wait staff make for a worthwhile visit.
An Italian restaurant serving pasta and pizza. The restaurant can get packed on Friday and Saturday nights, at which time reservations are recommended.

Buddhist ascetics and quirky jazz pianists alike will feel at home at this cozy "slow food" restaurant. The fare is organically-grown, mostly vegetarian/vegan home-style Japanese. When you sit down, the owner will almost certainly ask…
This is a very large yakiniku place. It has patchwork architecture and tasty meat.
Okinawa-themed restaurant and bar. Head downstairs for the Hawaiian-themed bar Jingle-Jangle.
This is a sushi restaurant that specializes in eel, as its name indicates.
A burger and beer joint with a large variety of burgers and international drinks. Run by Village Vanguard, a chain of variety/bookstores.

Enjoy the company of this cafe's 15 cats as you sip your coffee or tea. An outlet for cat lovers who don't or can't keep cats at home, this cafe was covered in news wire reports in late 2007. Has another branch at Shinjuku.
Beans roasted to order, nicely-made lights sweets and a blend coffee to rival them all. Quiet, bright and popular.
A live house with recording studios available for booking.

Formerly the annex of Warp, now independent. Musicians such as Inushiki and Latyr Sy gather there, and collaborate until the brink of dawn. Time spent there is to experience musical and artistic genius.
A large club and live house. 2 floors and stage.
A cozy Brazilian-style luncheonette and bar with good food and live music.
An English-style pub with locations throughout Japan.
This is a famous and very tasty Hokkaido-style miso ramen shop. The "Oyaji Set" is notable.
Good ramen.
Famous for its salt ramen.
A rare ramen made with pineapple.
Spicy ramen is the specialty of this shop.
This is a restaurant specializing in soy sauce dishes, a rarity.
Horsemeat dishes are available at affordable prices.
A yakitori restaurant. All the clerks are friendly and nice. They serve good yakitori and sake.
A cafe where you can enjoy Japanese sweets in a relaxed atmosphere.
A large variety of desserts.
All-you-can-eat Kentucky Fried Chicken. Some of the menu items are only available here.
All you can eat shabu-shabu and sukiyaki. Ninety minutes of greatness.

eat.pr: Four pieces for ¥340, five pieces for ¥510
eat.b: Serves Chinese steamed dumplings (shoronpo).

The famous American restaurant chain, one of a few locations in the Tokyo area. This is a great place to have lunch, or some after-work happy hour drinks (half-price on weekdays between 16:00 and 19:00). Staff are friendly, and the…

A branch of the popular chain of English pubs found all around Tokyo and other urban centers across Japan. Lively atmosphere especially on weekends. Reasonably priced drinks along with a decent selection of British pub fare, as well as…

The entrance is a little difficult to find, but what do you expect from a restaurant designed like a hidden ninja fortress? Navigate through dark corridors, over bridges and trap doors to your hidden room, where ninja waiters attend to…
Specializes in kushiage, counter in a very Japanese cozy atmosphere.
Their speciality (and only dish) is the Seolleongtang soup, a white broth with beef, served with many side dishes including kimchi. Add salt and pepper yourself to the soup at your convenience.

eat.pr: Somewhat expensive even for Tokyo standards
eat.b: Very good selection of imported foods.
Chain fast food restaurant selling gyudon beef bowls. Meals start from around ¥400-500

eat.pr: Basic tendon bowl costs ¥560, a steal by any standard
eat.b: Cheap fast-food tempura.

A tiny place, convenient for anyone staying there. Serves Japanese and foreign food. The owner, Yuki, is a former backpacker and will happily give advice on choosing the right sho-chu from a selection of 60 kinds. Try the raw octopus…
It is a donkatsu shop in Akihabara. It sells high-quality donkatsu even if there is a small amount of money.

This maid cafe has card games, drinks, food, and young women dressed up as maids to serve you. If you order an omelet, they'll draw a picture of a cute animal on the top in ketchup. In addition to this shop, there are 3 branch stores…
The original and not quite as over-the-top (or expensive) as some of the competition. A long line can form on weekends.

eat.pr: ¥500 for first 30 minutes; ¥150 for each ten minutes; drinks ¥300 to
eat.b: A 'cat cafe': you play with the shop's (very clean) cats while drinking tea. You'll be asked to remove your shoes and wash your hands on entry. You'll also be gently pressured to order one of their drinks. It's a different experience.
This place has been making "melon pan" since 1945, and they haven't changed the decoration. It is a buttery and milky small cake with a crispy sweet crust.
Freshly grilled taiyaki, a traditional sweet waffle in the shape of a lucky fish, with your choice of red bean, sweet potato or custard filling.

After an exhausting day visiting the temples, grab some hot steamed dumplings outside, or step inside for traditional desserts such as oshiruko (grilled rice cake in a sweet-bean porridge) or cream an-mitsu (gelatin cubes in molasses…
Over 150 years of history. Try their tempura and soba set! Or the fresh deep fried flour/batter at the front of the restaurant. You can smell them from a mile away, because they use sesame oil.
Good tempura in a convenient location, with fifty years of history behind it.

Ludicrously fluffy pancakes served in wobbly stacks of three, with a selection of sweet and savoury toppings. Extremely popular among the Instagram crowd, the only way to get a guaranteed seat is to queue up in person before 8:30am and…
One of Tokyo's most famous tempura restaurants, opened in 1887. Be prepared for extremely long queues during meal times. An English menu is available on request.

Another local institution, Komagata has been serving up loach hotpot (dojō nabe) for over 200 years. Small, bony and slimy, loach was the working man's alternative to eel, then as now an expensive luxury. It's a bit of an acquired taste…

Lurking in the dingy/atmospheric "mole alley" under Tobu Asakusa station, this friendly joint serves up yakitori grilled chicken skewers and, incongruously, a limited menu of Italian favorites. Try the tsukimi tsukune, a giant chicken…

Classic tonkatsu pork cutlets deep-fried to perfection, with your choice of fatty rōsu or leaner hire. Limited but extremely popular lunch menu (expect to queue for up to an hour), dinner menu has more options like katsu curry and katsudon.
One of the longer-running operators, with set meals of sashimi and tempura and daily departures sailing a loop from Asakusa to Odaiba and back.

This tiny 8-seater restaurant has had a Michelin star for 13 years running thanks to its uncompromisingly old-school Edo-style sushi, prepared with seasonal seafood and akasu red vinegar made from sake lees. Reserve well in advance.

The home of the Denki Bran cocktail, this was Japan's first Western-style bar when it first opened in 1880 and remains a truly local institution. The ground floor is a large beer-hall-like bar, the second is a Western-style restaurant,…
Asakusa Naniwaya branch the original of Taiyaki Naniwaya Sohonten (Azabu Jyu-ban). You can enjoy green tea and coffee at the cafe in the shop, with all handmade Japanese sweets.
A popular hamburger restaurant decorated with American memorabilia.
Serves kushiage (deep fried skewered food) in a rare old wooden building.

Obsessively perfectionist handmade soba noodles for connoisseurs, made using only buckwheat from a certain village in Hokkaido and rolled on the thighs of virgins — or at least that's what you'd expect from the price. Their famous…
Restaurant with amazing views of Imperial Palace and excellent service. Lunch seems the best value. Kobe beef from ¥23,500. Dress code: casual.
For lunch you should get a bowl of rice with mentaiko (semi-spicy red fish eggs). Their specialty for dinner is motsunabe (tripe hotpot).
Yabu Soba opened its doors for business in 1880.
